questions.prompt: Compute \(\det\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: For \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), the determinant is \(ad-bc\). Here \[\det=4\cdot3-1\cdot2=12-2=10.\]

questions.prompt: Can the determinant of a \(2\times3\) matrix be computed? Explain briefly.
questions.answer: No. Determinants are defined only for square matrices. A \(2\times3\) matrix is not square, so \(\det(A)\) is not defined.

questions.prompt: Find \(\det\begin{pmatrix}-2&5\\3&1\end{pmatrix}\).
For first-row cofactor expansion of a \(3\times3\) matrix, what signs multiply the three first-row minors?
questions.answer: The cofactor signs alternate across the first row as \(+,-,+\). Thus \[\det(A)=a_{11}M_{11}-a_{12}M_{12}+a_{13}M_{13}.\]

questions.prompt: Compute \(\det\begin{pmatrix}6&-1\\4&2\end{pmatrix}\) and state whether the corresponding square system has a unique solution.
questions.answer: The determinant is \[6\cdot2-(-1)\cdot4=12+4=16.\] Since \(16\ne0\), the square system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\) has a unique solution for every compatible \(\mathbf b\).

questions.prompt: Compute \(\det\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&3&4\\0&0&5\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: This matrix is upper triangular, so its determinant is the product of the diagonal entries: \[\det=1\cdot3\cdot5=15.\]

questions.prompt: Expand along the first row to compute \(\det\begin{pmatrix}2&0&1\\3&4&5\\1&-2&0\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: Use \(+,-,+\) along the first row. The middle term is zero. \[\det=2\det\begin{pmatrix}4&5\\-2&0\end{pmatrix}+1\det\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}.\] The minors are \(4\cdot0-5(-2)=10\) and \(3(-2)-4(1)=-10\). Hence \[\det=2(10)+(-10)=10.\]

questions.prompt: Compute \(\det\begin{pmatrix}0&2&1\\1&3&0\\4&-1&2\end{pmatrix}\) by first-row expansion.
questions.answer: First-row expansion gives \[\det=0M_{11}-2M_{12}+1M_{13}.\] Now \(M_{12}=\det\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\4&2\end{pmatrix}=2\), and \(M_{13}=\det\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\4&-1\end{pmatrix}=1(-1)-3(4)=-13\). Therefore \[\det=-2(2)+1(-13)=-4-13=-17.\]

questions.prompt: Compute \(\det\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\0&-1&4\\2&1&0\end{pmatrix}\) by expanding along the first row.
questions.answer: Expand along the first row: \[\det=1\det\begin{pmatrix}-1&4\\1&0\end{pmatrix}-2\det\begin{pmatrix}0&4\\2&0\end{pmatrix}+3\det\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}.\] The minors are \(-4\), \(-8\), and \(2\). Thus \[\det=1(-4)-2(-8)+3(2)=-4+16+6=18.\]

questions.prompt: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&3&2\\0&4&1\end{pmatrix}\), compute \(\det(A)\) and decide whether \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\) has a unique solution for every \(\mathbf b\in\mathbb R^3\).
questions.answer: Expand along the first row: \[\det(A)=2\det\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\4&1\end{pmatrix}-1\det\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] The minors are \(3\cdot1-2\cdot4=-5\) and \(1\cdot1-2\cdot0=1\). Hence \[\det(A)=2(-5)-1=-11.\] Since \(-11\ne0\), the system has a unique solution for every \(\mathbf b\in\mathbb R^3\).

questions.prompt: Show by determinant calculation that the columns of \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&6\end{pmatrix}\) cannot give a unique solution matrix.
questions.answer: The determinant is \[1\cdot6-2\cdot3=6-6=0.\] A zero determinant means the square matrix is singular. Therefore the system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\) does not have a unique solution for every \(\mathbf b\). Geometrically, the second column is twice the first, so the columns do not provide two independent directions.

questions.prompt: A student computes \(\det\begin{pmatrix}2&5\\7&1\end{pmatrix}=2\cdot5-7\cdot1\). Correct the computation.
questions.answer: The formula is \(ad-bc\), not \(ab-cd\). Here \(a=2\), \(b=5\), \(c=7\), and \(d=1\). So \[\det=2\cdot1-5\cdot7=2-35=-33.\] The student's multiplication paired entries from columns incorrectly.

questions.prompt: Find all values of \(k\) such that \(\det\begin{pmatrix}k&2\\8&k\end{pmatrix}=0\).
questions.answer: Compute the determinant: \[\det=k\cdot k-2\cdot8=k^2-16.\] Set it equal to zero: \[k^2-16=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad (k-4)(k+4)=0.\] Therefore \(k=4\) or \(k=-4\).

questions.prompt: For \(A(k)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&k\\2&1&3\\0&4&1\end{pmatrix}\), find \(k\) such that \(\det(A(k))=0\).
questions.answer: Expand along the first row: \[\det(A)=1\det\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\4&1\end{pmatrix}+k\det\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&4\end{pmatrix}.\] The first minor is \(1-12=-11\). The second minor is \(8-0=8\). Thus \[\det(A)=-11+8k.\] Set this equal to zero: \(-11+8k=0\), so \(k=\frac{11}{8}\).

questions.prompt: For \(A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}t&1&0\\0&t&1\\0&0&t-2\end{pmatrix}\), find the parameter values for which \(\det(A(t))\ne0\).
questions.answer: The matrix is upper triangular, so \[\det(A(t))=t\cdot t\cdot(t-2)=t^2(t-2).\] This is nonzero when neither factor is zero. Hence \(t\ne0\) and \(t\ne2\). For those values the matrix has nonzero determinant.

questions.prompt: A \(3\times3\) determinant is expanded along a row containing two zeros. Explain why this is usually a good strategy, and compute \(\det\begin{pmatrix}0&0&5\\1&2&3\\4&0&-1\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: Expansion along a row with zeros removes terms because each zero multiplies its minor. Expand along the first row: \[\det=5\det\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\4&0\end{pmatrix}.\] The sign for position \((1,3)\) is positive. The minor is \(1\cdot0-2\cdot4=-8\). Therefore \[\det=5(-8)=-40.\]

questions.prompt: Prove from the \(2\times2\) determinant formula that two proportional columns give determinant zero.
questions.answer: Let the first column be \(\begin{pmatrix}a\\c\end{pmatrix}\) and let the second column be \(\lambda\begin{pmatrix}a\\c\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda a\\lambda c\end{pmatrix}\). The matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}a&\lambda a\\c&\lambda c\end{pmatrix}\). Its determinant is \[a(\lambda c)-(\lambda a)c=\lambda ac-\lambda ac=0.\] Thus proportional columns force the determinant to be zero.

questions.prompt: A student says \(\det(A)=0\) means \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\) has no solution. Explain the precise conclusion instead.
questions.answer: The precise conclusion is that the square system does not have a unique solution for every compatible \(\mathbf b\). When \(\det(A)=0\), the matrix is singular. Depending on \(\mathbf b\), the system may have no solution or infinitely many solutions. The determinant alone rules out the guaranteed unique-solution case; it does not decide consistency for every right-hand side.

questions.prompt: Explain why checking that a matrix is square is not a cosmetic step before computing a determinant.
questions.answer: The determinant is a function defined on square matrices because its geometric and algebraic meanings compare equal-dimensional input and output spaces. The cofactor formula also requires deleting one row and one column from a square matrix to produce smaller square minors. For a non-square matrix, these structures do not apply, so writing \(\det(A)\) is undefined rather than merely hard to compute.
